lines: It's seven forty in the morning, and Priya types: small balcony garden.
Billions of pins exist. A few dozen will reach her screen.
Search works like a funnel. Retrieval grabs about a hundred thousand pins.
Pre-ranking has milliseconds to cut them to about a thousand.
Heavy ranking models pick the last hundred.
This Pinterest paper is about that middle step.
The usual tool is a two tower model: two clerks who never talk.
One writes a card about Priya and her search.
The other has already written a card for every pin, ahead of time.
The score is how well the two cards line up.
Lining up means a dot product: multiply matching entries, then add.
Say Priya's card reads point eight, point one, point five. A herb box pin reads point nine, zero, point four.
Point seven two, plus zero, plus point two: a match of point nine two.
Real cards hold sixty four numbers. The sum works the same way.
It's fast, because every pin's card is ready before she searches.
But the clerks never meet. Neither can know that people who typed these exact words kept saving this exact pin.
So InteractRank pastes a guestbook on the back of each pin.
For each past search, it counts how often people engaged with this pin.
In symbols: engagements with this pin for this search, divided by how often the search was made.
Say balcony garden was searched a thousand times, and this pin was saved or opened on a hundred and twenty. Point one two.
Counts are kept over seven days, ninety days, one year, and two years, and can be split by groups like country.
Each pin keeps only its most engaging searches, and new days are simply added to the old counts.
The final score blends the clerks and the guestbook.
A learned weight on the card match, plus a learned weight on each guestbook line.
With example weights: one times point nine two, plus three times point one two. One point two eight.
Another pin matches the cards better, at one point oh, but nobody saved it for this search. It stays at one point oh, below.
The guestbook is looked up, not computed, so this adds almost no work.
Priya's card also reads her last hundred actions across Pinterest, updated in real time.
One summary is a learned weighted average. A second lets the search decide what matters.
Rate three past saves for garden: point nine, point six, and zero.
With search weights of point six, point three, and point one, her garden interest is point seven two.
It learns from past searches: was this pin saved, or opened for a long look?
Pins borrowed from other searches serve as obvious wrong answers, so it also learns what doesn't fit.
Offline, it put the right pin in the top three two point nine percent more often than plain two towers.
A heavier rival, IntTower, gained less, using over three thousand operations. InteractRank uses one hundred forty two.
Then a week-long test with ten million users, against the old word-matching ranker, BM25.
Sessions where people found what they wanted: two towers alone, up two point seven percent. Guestbooks alone, three point six.
Together, six point five. That's three point seven over two towers.
Guestbooks shine on popular searches: plus five point nine percent on their own.
On searches almost nobody repeats, the guestbook is nearly empty, and alone it does no better than the old ranker.
With the towers beside it, InteractRank beats both, in every group.
Back in Priya's kitchen, the herb box is near the top.
Two clerks who never meet, and a guestbook of what people actually saved.
InteractRank now runs Pinterest search worldwide, billions of searches a day.
